beats.say: A New Mexico rancher rode out across his ranch, and found shiny wreckage scattered all over the ground.
beats.headline: WHAT CRASHED?
beats.short_title: What REALLY Crashed at Roswell? 👽 Case #3
beats.comment: What did you think crashed? 👽 aliens / 🎈 balloon
beats.bonus: Project Mogul's balloon trains carried microphones to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The Air Force's reports came out in 1994 and 1997.
beats.caption: What really crashed at Roswell in 1947? The cover-up was real. The aliens weren't. What did you guess? 👽 aliens / 🎈 balloon #roswell #ufo #history #meatballinvestigates Follow Meatball for a new case every day 🍝
sources: US Air Force, 'The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert' (1995) and 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' (1997): the debris came from Project Mogul, a classified balloon train carrying sensors to detect Soviet nuclear tests; the 'alien body' stories were explained as anthropomorphic test dummies from 1950s high-altitude drops — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mogul (checked 2026-10-26)

Wikipedia, Roswell incident (rancher W. W. 'Mac' Brazel found debris in June-July 1947; 8 July 1947 RAAF press release announced a recovered 'flying disc'; the next day Gen. Roger Ramey said it was a weather balloon; interest revived in the late 1970s) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_incident

beats.say: Foil, sticks, tape, rubber. So what really crashed? Guess.
Subscribe. I investigate a weird case every day.
See, in July 1947, the Army base at Roswell put out a press release. They said they'd recovered a flying disc.
The next day, a general posed with the pieces and said, never mind, it's a weather balloon.
Guess one: a flying saucer, and the bodies were hidden. That's what the books said decades later.
Guess two: a plain weather balloon, exactly what the Army said. That's not it either.
So I went to check Area 51 myself. Bad idea. They do not do tours.
Wait. Here's the weird part. The balloon story was a cover story too.
Verdict: a secret spy balloon. Project Mogul. A long train of balloons carrying microphones, to hear Soviet nuclear tests.
It was top secret, so nobody could say what it really was. For decades.
The Air Force finally explained it in 1994. Then came the alien bodies.
Their answer? Crash test dummies, dropped from the sky in the 1950s.
So the cover-up was real. The aliens weren't.
And the name of the Air Force's last report on it? Case Closed. It did not close the case.
